# Jonah 2: Research notes

**What's missing.** I ran out of research tool calls before I could read Gill and the Pulpit Commentary in full, or any NET Bible notes. I found nothing from Lutheran sites (lcms.org, 1517.org) or Wesleyan sites. Clarke's Methodist commentary page would not load, so I only have a short excerpt from it. I found nothing from Orthodox (oca.org) or newadvent.org sources, and nothing from prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teachers. None of those appear below.

---

## Whole chapter

- **Ellicott:** The chapter is really a psalm of thanksgiving. It is introduced the same way as Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jonah-2.html
- **Use of the Psalms.** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB) say Jonah identifies himself with the saints of old, appropriating their experiences as recorded in the Word of God. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/jonah-2.html
  - The Pulpit Commentary says the shared wording proves nothing about when the book was written, because like circumstances call forth like expressions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/2.htm
- **Modern scholarship (reported second-hand, by conservative writers):**
  - Constable says many critical scholars date this prophecy in the postexilic period during the time of Ezra and Nehemiah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jonah.html
  - Coffman reports that some call the psalm an ill-fitting addition to the narrative that was not part of the original book. He rejects this. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/jonah-2.html
- **Bible Odyssey (modern scholarship):** Early readers worried less about whether a person could survive inside a fish. Jewish, Christian and Muslim interpreters focused instead on providence, the role of a prophet, and Jonah as a forerunner of Jesus. https://concordiatheology.bibleodyssey.org/articles/interpretations-of-jonah/
- **A dissenting evangelical view (Bob Deffinbaugh, bible.org):** He argues the psalm differ[s] from the real Psalms. He calls it an example of superficial and synthetic spirituality, which goes against the usual warm reading. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-prodigal-prophet-jonah-21-10

## v. 1

- **When did Jonah pray?** Teachers disagree.
  - Guzik (Enduring Word, Calvary Chapel) thinks Jonah apparently did nothing for the three days and prayed only afterward. He adds that the opening of the prayer may show Jonah had been crying out all along, and that this prayer came after God assured him he would be delivered. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-2/
  - Piper (Desiring God, Baptist) says the chapter is what Jonah prayed while still conscious in the fish. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/cry-of-distress-and-voice-of-thanks
  - The Pulpit Commentary says these were his feelings while sinking and while trapped, and he may have put them into poetic form after he was rescued. https://biblehub.com/jonah/2-1.htm
- **"His God."** A Biblical Illustrator sermon notes that Jonah prays to the God of the covenant. It calls this the prayer of an appropriating faith. https://biblehub.com/sermons/jonah/2-1.htm
- **The fish as a burial.** The Bible Hub study notes say Jonah's confinement was like a burial, which looks ahead to Jesus' use of Jonah in Matthew 12:40. https://biblehub.com/jonah/2-1.htm

## v. 2

- **"Belly of Sheol."**
  - Ellicott calls it a forcible figure for imminent death. He says "underworld" translates *sheôl* better than "hell" or "grave." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jonah-2.html
  - Keil and Delitzsch say the phrase is not to be taken as the shark's belly, as Jerome supposes. For them it is a poetic picture of deadly danger with no apparent way out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/2-2.htm
  - Gill reads it as the fish's belly, which was like a grave to Jonah. He adds that it may also describe the terror in Jonah's conscience. Gill notes that Calvin rendered the phrase "belly of the grave" (*e ventre sepulchri*). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jonah/2-2.htm
  - Clarke (Methodist) says that here *sheol* must mean the bottom of the sea. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/jonah-2.html
- **Did Jonah actually die? A debated popular view.**
  - One devotional on Precept Austin says Jonah may actually have died and gone to "hell." https://www.preceptaustin.org/jonah-devotionals-and-sermon-illustrations
  - Lowell Johnson suggests Jonah's body was in the fish while his soul was in Sheol. https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons-on-jonah-lowell-johnson
  - Deffinbaugh disagrees. He says Jonah was "as good as dead" and that whether he died is not the point. https://bible.org/seriespage/psalm-prodigal-prophet-jonah-21-10
- **Answered before rescue.** Guzik says Jonah knew God had heard him before the answer came, which shows his faith. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-2/
- **Answers come in stages.** Piper says God answers in stages: the fish was the first stage of the rescue and a guarantee of dry land. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/cry-of-distress-and-voice-of-thanks

## v. 3

- **God did the casting.**
  - Guzik: Jonah saw that God himself, not the sailors, had thrown him into the sea. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-2/
  - Spurgeon (Baptist): the word implies God had thrown Jonah violently, like something tossed overboard. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-exposition-jonah
- **"Your breakers and waves."**
  - The Pulpit Commentary: the line comes from Psalm 42:7. Jonah takes what the psalm says as a metaphor and applies it to what literally happened to him. Saying "your" billows admits God's hand in the punishment. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/2.htm
  - Ellicott: "floods" literally means "river," used here of ocean currents. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jonah-2.html
- **Picture of Christ.** Precept Austin's devotional material treats this storm as a picture of Jesus, who could also say "all thy waves… are gone over me." https://www.preceptaustin.org/jonah-devotionals-and-sermon-illustrations

## v. 4

- **"Banished from your sight."** Ellicott, quoting Pusey: Jonah had chosen to leave God's presence, and now God seemed to take him at his word. Jonah strengthens David's "I am cut off" (Psalm 31:22) to "I am cast forth." "Look again toward your temple" sounds like the hope of an exile, turning toward the temple to pray. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jonah-2.html
- **Faith over despair.**
  - The Pulpit Commentary: Jonah first expected to die, but faith and hope soon triumphed over despondency. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/2.htm
  - Spurgeon compares this to Job's "Though he slay me." Even if God does not look at him, Jonah will look toward where God lives. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-exposition-jonah
  - Guzik: Jonah's worst pain was being separated from God, not the disaster itself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-2/

## v. 5

- **Ellicott:** The seaweed detail is quite original. He also notes that the psalm never mentions the fish. Its focus is on the fact of Jonah's escape, not the way it happened. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jonah-2.html

## v. 6

- **"Roots of the mountains."** Ellicott: Hebrews pictured mountains as pillars of the world standing in the sea. Their hidden bases were the edge of the earth, close to the world of the dead. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jonah-2.html
- **"Barred in forever."** The Pulpit Commentary: the gate back to life was locked behind him. "Forever" is how it looked, since he had no power to return. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/jonah/2.htm
- **"The pit."**
  - A Precept Austin note says the Hebrew means destruction or decay, as in Psalm 16:10. The Greek Old Testament (Septuagint) translates it "corruption." https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_820-21
  - JFB: Jonah speaks as if his rescue were already happening. They also think Hezekiah echoed Jonah's words in Isaiah 38:17. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jon/Jon_002.cfm

## v. 7

- **"Fading away."** Ellicott: literally the soul "covered itself," picturing the mist of death closing over sight and senses. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jonah-2.html
- **Remembering God.**
  - JFB: this shows the triumph of spirit over flesh, of faith over sense. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfb/jonah-2.html
  - Spurgeon: memory usually fails when the heart faints, but Jonah remembered God. Though cast from God's sight, his prayer reached God's temple. https://www.preceptaustin.org/spurgeons-exposition-jonah
  - Constable: even though Jonah felt far from God, his prayer reached God's heavenly dwelling. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jonah-2.html

## v. 8

- **"Loving devotion."** The Berean Study Bible footnote explains that the Hebrew word *chesed* covers love, kindness, faithfulness and mercy, and loyalty to a covenant. https://biblehub.com/jonah/2.htm
- **What they forsake.**
  - Ellicott: idolaters give up their own share of covenant grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jonah-2.html
  - JFB reads "mercy" as God himself, and applies it to Jonah: he had "forsaken his own mercy" by running to lands where idols were worshipped. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/jfb/Jon/Jon_002.cfm
  - Guzik: Jonah saw that running from God was like being an idolater. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-2/

## v. 9

- **Sacrifice and vows.**
  - Ellicott: Jonah has sinned but is still one of the covenant people, and sacrifice can formally restore him. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/jonah-2.html
  - Constable: Jonah now does what the sailors already did in 1:16. He quotes a writer who calls it ironic that Jonah is at last brought to the point the Gentile seamen have already reached. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/jonah-2.html
- **What kind of "salvation"? Commentators differ.**
  - Utley (bible.org) says the Hebrew word mainly means physical rescue here, not salvation in the New Testament sense. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21254
  - A sermon listed on Bible Hub cites Gill: the spelling of the word points to eternal salvation of the soul. https://biblehub.com/sermons/jonah/2-2.htm
  - Guzik takes it both ways: Jonah's own rescue, and the wider truth that salvation does not belong to any nation or race. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-2/
- **Repentance.** Guzik lists signs of Jonah's real repentance and calls repentance both an event and a process. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-2/

## v. 10

- **God commands the fish.**
  - Guzik: the fish obeyed God both in swallowing and in releasing Jonah. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-2/
  - Guzik on the "three days" (Matthew 12:40): he cites Jewish usage in which part of a day counted as a whole day. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-2/
  - Guzik on where Jonah landed: Scripture does not say it was near Nineveh, which is about 375 miles from the Mediterranean. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/jonah-2/
- **Catholic reading:** A Catholic Answers talk says the most obvious meaning of the sign of Jonah is Christ's death and resurrection. https://www.catholic.com/audio/sp/what-you-missed-about-jonah-and-christs-passion-and-resurrection
- **Early church:** Bible Odyssey reports that Cyril of Alexandria (5th century) saw the mystery of Christ foreshadowed in Jonah's story. https://concordiatheology.bibleodyssey.org/articles/interpretations-of-jonah/
